record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: What fraction of massive binaries merge before core hydrogen burning, during the pre-main-sequence phase, because residual accretion and tides from circum-binary material shrink their orbits? If such mergers are common, can massive stars on the long-lived core-hydrogen-burning main sequence be observationally separated into a population formed mainly by disk accretion and a population that gained much of their mass through binary merger, for example through distinctive stellar-spin signatures?

evidence.quote: 2.1. Which fraction of binaries merge as pre-main sequence stars?
The question is whether we can recognise this dichotomy in the long lived core-hydrogen burning state. One stellar quantity which may contain a memory of the formation process is the stellar spin.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider massive binary star systems (with at least one component of mass ≳ 8 solar masses) formed via disk fragmentation or capture and still embedded in circum-binary material during the pre-main-sequence phase. Residual accretion from this material and tidal interactions with it can extract orbital angular momentum and shrink the binary's orbit, in some cases driving the two components to coalesce before either star settles onto the core-hydrogen-burning main sequence.

(a) Determine the fraction f_pre-MS of massive binaries that merge during the pre-main-sequence phase (i.e., before the onset of stable core hydrogen burning in both components) as a consequence of residual disk accretion and circum-binary tidal torques.

(b) Assuming such pre-main-sequence mergers occur frequently, decide whether the population of stars observed on the long-lived core-hydrogen-burning main sequence can be partitioned, by means of observable stellar properties, into two distinct subpopulations: (i) stars that acquired the bulk of their mass through accretion from a protostellar disk without a merger, and (ii) stars that acquired a significant fraction of their final mass through a pre-main-sequence binary merger. In particular, determine whether the surface rotational velocity (stellar spin) — or some other observable retaining memory of the formation channel — provides a statistically reliable discriminator between these two channels.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2023–2025) continues to investigate massive-binary merger fractions and the role of stellar spin/magnetism as merger signatures, with estimates that ~10–25% of massive stars merge with a companion, but no consensus on the specific pre-main-sequence merger fraction or on a robust observational discriminator separating disk-accretion-formed from merger-formed main-sequence massive stars. The question therefore appears still open.

status_evidence.title: Testing the role of merging binaries in the formation of the split main sequence in young clusters
status_evidence.snippet: Investigates whether binary mergers explain split main sequences in young clusters; merger products and their spin/rotation signatures remain under active study.
status_evidence.claim: Discriminating merger products from non-merger massive main-sequence stars via rotation/spin is still an active, unresolved research topic.

status_evidence.title: Evidence for stellar mergers of evolved massive binaries
status_evidence.snippet: Recent observational work proposing merger signatures in evolved massive binaries.
status_evidence.claim: Merger fractions and signatures for massive stars remain under investigation.

status_evidence.title: Stellar mergers as the origin of magnetic massive stars
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes pre-MS / MS mergers as origin of magnetic massive stars; predicted merger fraction ~10%.
status_evidence.claim: The merger fraction and its observational signatures (e.g., magnetism, spin) remain debated.
